# Strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking

Lecture 26 · [Original notes](https://www.alucasphys.com/p7810s2026/p7810s2026_lecture26.pdf)

::: {.callout-tip title="Learning objectives"}
Distinguish strong and weak symmetry of a density matrix; understand the thermodynamic-limit qualification in ensemble equivalence; rewrite diffusion in doubled phase variables; explain how charge leakage gaps a diffusion mode; recognize the roles of unitarity, positivity, and thermal KMS symmetry.
:::

## Why revisit an ordinary diffusion equation? {#sec-l26-question}

Diffusion is familiar: a conserved density spreads with $\omega=-iDk^2$. The interpretation explored here is more recent. A density matrix has separate ket and bra actions of a symmetry, providing a richer symmetry-breaking structure than a single classical order parameter.

The connection between that structure and hydrodynamics is developed in the primary paper by Huang, Qi, Zhang, and Lucas, [*Physical Review B* **111**, 125147 (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.111.125147), with [open full text](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.08760v2). In its effective theory, finite susceptibility characterizes strong-to-weak breaking, and the diffusion excitation plays the associated Goldstone role. This is a modern interpretation of the hydrodynamic action under stated symmetry and equilibrium assumptions. The standard diffusion equation and the density-matrix identities below do not depend on adopting a particular terminology for mixed-state phases.

## Pure states, cats, and local order {#sec-l26-pure}

A pure state is symmetric under $U(g)$ when $U(g)|\psi\rangle=e^{i\alpha(g)}|\psi\rangle$. Conventional spontaneous symmetry breaking is diagnosed in a thermodynamic phase by order and locally distinguishable symmetry-related states, with care about the infinite-volume limit. A symmetric finite-size cat state can still have long-range correlations.

For example, let $X=\prod_iX_i$ flip every qubit, and take

$$
|\mathrm{cat}\rangle=\frac{|0\cdots0\rangle+|1\cdots1\rangle}{\sqrt2}.
$$

It satisfies $X|\mathrm{cat}\rangle=|\mathrm{cat}\rangle$, $\langle Z_i\rangle=0$, and $\langle Z_iZ_j\rangle=1$. Tracing out one qubit removes the coherence between the two branches and gives an equal mixture of all-zero and all-one states on the others. Every fixed small collection of qubits has the same reduced state in that mixture as in the cat. Thus one-point invariance is not enough to decide whether a thermodynamic state has conventional order; long-distance correlations and the limiting procedure matter.

This example is preparatory. It illustrates why replacing a state-vector test by a naive density-matrix test can conceal important distinctions.

## Strong and weak symmetry are different algebraic statements {#sec-l26-density}

To avoid confusing the density operator with a local density, write the former as $\varrho$ and the latter as $n$. For a unitary $U$, define strong symmetry of the state by

$$
U\varrho=e^{i\alpha}\varrho,
$$ {#eq-l26-strong}

and weak symmetry by

$$
U\varrho U^\dagger=\varrho.
$$ {#eq-l26-weak}

Hermiticity gives the corresponding right-action relation from @eq-l26-strong, so strong symmetry implies weak symmetry. For $U(\theta)=e^{i\theta Q}$, strong symmetry means the support of $\varrho$ lies in one charge eigenspace. Weak symmetry only says that $\varrho$ is block diagonal in charge; different blocks may occur with different weights.

For example, consider the fixed-charge and charge-fluctuating states

$$
\varrho_{Q_0}=\frac{P_{Q_0}e^{-\beta H}}{Z_{Q_0}},\qquad
\varrho_\mu=\frac{e^{-\beta(H-\mu Q)}}{Z_\mu},\qquad[H,Q]=0.
$$ {#eq-l26-ensembles}

The first satisfies $e^{i\theta Q}\varrho_{Q_0}=e^{i\theta Q_0}\varrho_{Q_0}$ and is strongly symmetric. The second is weakly symmetric and, when more than one charge sector is populated, not strongly symmetric. A charge-only weight $e^{-\lambda Q}$, as used for the schematic example in the lecture, has the same algebraic distinction. Normalization and trace convergence must be supplied in any microscopic implementation.

Thermodynamic ensemble equivalence concerns local observables when $Q_0$ and $\mu$ are chosen to match density, subject to the usual thermodynamic hypotheses. It does not assert equality of the full density matrices. In particular, total-charge variance is zero in one ensemble and generally extensive in the other. Global constraints survive even when local measurements cannot distinguish ensembles.

::: {.callout-note title="What the word spontaneous adds"}
Equations @eq-l26-strong and @eq-l26-weak classify a given finite density matrix algebraically. A spontaneous-breaking claim additionally specifies the symmetry of the dynamics, the thermodynamic state family, and a suitable order diagnostic or thermodynamic-limit construction. The lecture interprets local relaxation from fixed-charge dynamics to a charge-fluctuating equilibrium description in this strong-to-weak framework. It is not a claim that unitary, charge-conserving evolution literally changes the total charge sector of a closed finite system.
:::

## From the MSR density action to two phase fields {#sec-l26-action}

Start with a conserved density $n$, its response field $\pi_n$, and a conjugate phase $\phi$ with response $\pi_\phi$. In a convenient convention the phase response imposes

$$
\partial_t\phi+\mu=0.
$$

When the equation of state is invertible, eliminate $n$ in favor of $\partial_t\phi$. Write $\phi_r=\phi$ and $\phi_a=\pi_n$. Near equilibrium, $\delta n=\chi\delta\mu=-\chi\partial_t\phi_r$. Up to integration by parts, the quadratic long-wavelength action is

$$
\mathcal L=\chi\partial_t\phi_a\partial_t\phi_r
-K\nabla\phi_a\cdot\nabla\phi_r
+iT\sigma\nabla\phi_a\cdot\nabla
(\phi_a+i\beta\partial_t\phi_r).
$$ {#eq-l26-action}

Here $\chi>0$, $\sigma\ge0$, and $K$ is the superfluid stiffness. These are auxiliary doubled fields in an effective description of response and fluctuations. The $a$ field is integrated over, even though its saddle imposes a physical equation; it should not be treated as an additional independent classical density.

For $K=0$, the action is invariant under

$$
\phi_a\mapsto\phi_a+c_a,\qquad
\phi_r\mapsto\phi_r+f(\mathbf x),
$$ {#eq-l26-normal-shifts}

where $f$ is arbitrary and time independent. A nonzero stiffness reduces the latter freedom to a constant shift. This recovers the normal-versus-superfluid distinction encountered previously. The shift of $\phi_a$ is associated with the strong symmetry in the doubled formulation; the physical-phase shift corresponds to the weak symmetry. Both constant shifts survive in the action even though the thermodynamic state can realize them spontaneously rather than linearly.

## Supplementary derivation: diffusion and charge leakage {#sec-l26-leakage}

Set $K=0$ and vary @eq-l26-action with respect to $\phi_a$, then set $\phi_a=0$. The deterministic equation is

$$
\chi\partial_t^2\phi_r-\sigma\nabla^2\partial_t\phi_r=0.
$$

Using $\delta n=-\chi\partial_t\phi_r$ gives

$$
\partial_t\delta n=D\nabla^2\delta n,\qquad D=\frac\sigma\chi.
$$ {#eq-l26-diffusion}

The arbitrary time-independent part of $\phi_r$ is redundant, which is why the phase equation contains an additional zero-frequency freedom rather than another physical normal-fluid mode.

Now let the system exchange charge with a reservoir. A local term

$$
\Delta\mathcal L=iT\gamma\phi_a(\phi_a+i\beta\partial_t\phi_r)
$$ {#eq-l26-bath}

breaks the constant $\phi_a$ shift explicitly while preserving the weak physical symmetry. The density equation becomes

$$
\partial_t\delta n=-\frac\gamma\chi\delta n+D\nabla^2\delta n,
\qquad\omega=-i\left(\frac\gamma\chi+Dk^2\right).
$$ {#eq-l26-gapped}

The former diffusion mode now relaxes even at $k=0$. This directly illustrates the distinction between spontaneous breaking, which can retain a gapless mode, and explicit violation of the conservation law. The noise part of @eq-l26-bath accompanies the leakage coefficient when the bath is thermal.

## Why the quantum contour has the same structure {#sec-l26-kms}

Density-matrix evolution has the form $U\varrho U^\dagger$, hence a forward and backward history. With contour fields $\phi_1,\phi_2$, a common convention is $\phi_r=(\phi_1+\phi_2)/2$ and $\phi_a=\phi_1-\phi_2$. Other normalizations of $\phi_a$ move factors of two. The essential requirements are

$$
S[\phi_r,\phi_a=0]=0,\qquad \operatorname{Im}S\ge0.
$$ {#eq-l26-sk-constraints}

The first follows from cancellation of identical forward and backward histories and expresses trace preservation; the second ensures that $e^{iS}$ is damped in noisy directions. A thermal initial state includes an imaginary-time segment of extent $\beta$. Cyclicity of the thermal trace produces the Kubo–Martin–Schwinger relation between differently ordered correlators.

Combining that relation with time reversal and expanding in small frequency gives a thermal transformation that shifts the response field by a term proportional to $-i\beta\partial_t\phi_r$. This is the origin of the MSR thermal time-reversal transformation and fluctuation–dissipation relation. At finite quantum frequency the contour transformation also corrects $\phi_r$ by a derivative of $\phi_a$; retaining only the classical low-frequency piece is an approximation. The response/noise construction is therefore consistent with, but does not require solving, the full microscopic quantum dynamics.

## Exercises and solutions {#sec-l26-exercises}

1. For $\varrho=p|0\rangle\langle0|+(1-p)|1\rangle\langle1|$ and $Q|q\rangle=q|q\rangle$, classify its symmetry when $0<p<1$.
2. Derive the uniform charge-relaxation time from @eq-l26-gapped.
3. Identify a global observable that distinguishes the two ensembles in @eq-l26-ensembles despite local equivalence.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
1. It commutes with $Q$, hence is weakly symmetric. Its two occupied charge sectors acquire different phases under left multiplication, so it is not strongly symmetric. At $p=0$ or $1$ it is strongly symmetric.
2. At $k=0$, $\delta n(t)=\delta n(0)e^{-\gamma t/\chi}$, giving $\tau_Q=\chi/\gamma$.
3. $\langle(Q-\langle Q\rangle)^2\rangle$ vanishes at fixed charge and is generally nonzero in the charge-fluctuating ensemble. It involves the entire system and is outside the local-observable equivalence statement.
:::
